scenes.text: Quick! How much do you spend on subscriptions every month? Guess. Out loud.
scenes.head: YOUR GUESS?

scenes.text: Got a number? Good. Hold on to it.
scenes.head: HOLD THAT NUMBER

scenes.text: Because in 2022, researchers asked Americans that exact question.
scenes.head: THE BIG GUESS
scenes.say: Because in twenty twenty-two, researchers asked Americans that exact question.
scenes.show_source: Source: C+R Research subscription survey, reported by CNBC (June 2, 2022)

scenes.text: On average, people guessed $86 a month. The real number? $219.
scenes.head: GUESS vs REALITY
scenes.say: On average, people guessed eighty-six dollars a month. The real number? ... Two hundred nineteen.
scenes.show_source: Source: C+R Research subscription survey, reported by CNBC (June 2, 2022)

scenes.text: Whoa! That's more than double!
scenes.head: MORE THAN DOUBLE

scenes.text: And 42% forgot about at least one subscription they were still paying for.
scenes.head: FORGOTTEN, BUT PAID
scenes.say: And forty-two percent forgot about at least one subscription they were still paying for.

scenes.text: Forty-two percent! That's not a subscription. That's a ghost.
scenes.head: 42% FORGOT

scenes.text: Here's the sneaky part. Ten dollars a month doesn't feel like money.
scenes.head: $10 A MONTH...
scenes.say: Here's the sneaky part. Ten dollars a month doesn't feel like money.

scenes.text: But ten dollars, twelve times? That's $120 a year. Same money. Different costume.
scenes.head: ...= $120 A YEAR
scenes.say: But ten dollars, twelve times? That's a hundred twenty dollars a year. Same money. Different costume.

scenes.text: Okay, okay... that was 2022. What about now?
scenes.head: WHAT ABOUT NOW?
scenes.say: Okay, okay... that was twenty twenty-two. What about now?

scenes.text: CNET's 2026 survey counted $111 a month.
scenes.head: 2026: $111 A MONTH
scenes.say: CNET's twenty twenty-six survey counted a hundred eleven dollars a month.
scenes.show_source: Source: CNET subscription survey, July 2026 (reported by WFSB, Jul 16, 2026)

scenes.text: Up from $90 a year before. That's 23% in one year.
scenes.head: +23% IN ONE YEAR
scenes.say: Up from ninety dollars a year before. That's twenty-three percent in one year.

scenes.text: And about $21 of it, every month? Stuff people don't even use.
scenes.head: $21 A MONTH. UNUSED.
scenes.say: And about twenty-one dollars of it, every month? Stuff people don't even use.

scenes.text: That's $252 a year. For nothing. Ow.
scenes.head: $252 A YEAR. FOR NOTHING.
scenes.say: That's two hundred fifty-two dollars a year. For nothing. Ow.
scenes.show_source: Source: CNET subscription survey, July 2026 (reported by WFSB, Jul 16, 2026)

scenes.text: Wait a second... why is that smaller than $219?
scenes.head: WAIT A SECOND...
scenes.say: Wait a second... why is that smaller than two hundred nineteen?

scenes.text: Different surveys count different things. Heh... but both say the same: it's more than we think.
scenes.head: TWO SURVEYS

scenes.text: So how does one tiny monthly charge turn into this? The trap has three doors.
scenes.head: THE TRAP HAS 3 DOORS

scenes.text: Door one: getting in is ridiculously easy. One click. Free trial. Done.
scenes.head: DOOR 1: EASY IN

scenes.text: Door two: you never decide to pay again. The card on file just... pays.
scenes.head: DOOR 2: AUTOPAY

scenes.text: And doors that stay open are powerful. Want proof from a totally different place?
scenes.head: DEFAULTS ARE POWERFUL

scenes.text: In a 2001 study, one company started signing new workers up for its 401(k) automatically.
scenes.head: THE DEFAULT TEST
scenes.say: In a two thousand one study, one company started signing new workers up for its four-oh-one-k automatically.
scenes.show_source: Source: Madrian & Shea, Quarterly Journal of Economics (2001)

scenes.text: Participation jumped from 37% to 86%. Same people. Same choice. Different default.
scenes.head: 37% TO 86%
scenes.say: Participation jumped from thirty-seven percent to eighty-six percent. Same people. Same choice. Different default.
scenes.show_source: Source: Madrian & Shea, Quarterly Journal of Economics (2001)

scenes.text: Defaults can help you save. Subscriptions use the exact same trick... to keep charging.
scenes.head: SAME TRICK

scenes.text: Door three: getting out. And that's where it gets weird.
scenes.head: DOOR 3: THE EXIT
